title: The Art of Remembering
context:
According to an ancient legend, the Greek poet Simonides was giving a speech at a banquet when he was called outside. While he was away, the roof of the hall collapsed, crushing the guests so badly that their relatives could not recognise them. Simonides, however, could name every victim, because he remembered where each had been sitting. The story may be invented, but it is said to have inspired the method of loci, a technique later used by Roman orators who needed to deliver long speeches without notes.

The method is simple. You select a place you know well, such as your home, and picture a route through it. Along the route, you place vivid images representing the things you want to remember: to recall a shopping list, you might imagine a giant loaf of bread blocking the front door and a goose sitting in the sink. To retrieve the list, you walk through the building in your mind and see what you find. Practitioners often compare the process to hanging coats on pegs in a hallway that they already know by heart. The technique works for two reasons. Human brains evolved to remember places, so locations provide a strong framework. And unusual, exaggerated images are easier to recall than abstract words.

Modern research has taken these claims seriously. Scientists studied people who compete in memory championships and found, perhaps surprisingly, that their brains were structurally normal and their intelligence scores were no higher than average. What distinguished them was that, when they memorised, regions linked with spatial memory became unusually active. Does that mean anyone can learn the skill? An experiment suggests so. Volunteers with ordinary memories trained for about forty minutes a day over six weeks, and the average number of words they could recall from a list of seventy-two rose from around twenty-six to around sixty-two, an improvement that was still visible four months later.

The method has limits, though. It is excellent for lists and sequences, such as the order of the planets or the items of a speech, but it does nothing to help a student understand why a historical event happened or how an equation works. Some educators therefore dismiss memorisation as an outdated habit. Others reply that facts stored in the mind are the raw material of creative thought, and that a person who must look everything up cannot easily make connections. Learning the technique also demands effort, since each route must be prepared and rehearsed, and using the same route again and again can lead to confusion between old and new images.

Two other strategies are supported by strong evidence. The first is spaced repetition. In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised long lists of nonsense syllables and discovered that forgetting is fastest soon after learning. Reviewing the material at increasing intervals, he found, flattens this curve, and many modern apps are built around the idea. The second is retrieval practice. Students who tested themselves on a text remembered more a week later than those who simply read it again, even though the re-readers felt more confident.

The methods are therefore best seen as complements rather than rivals. A memory palace gives structure to facts that must be learned in order; spacing and self-testing help them last. None of them replaces understanding, but a mind that is trained to hold information reliably has more room to think about what that information means.

questions.prompt: How was Simonides able to name the victims of the collapse?
options: By recognising their clothing
By reading the names on their seats
By remembering where each person had been sitting
By asking their relatives
questions.answer: By remembering where each person had been sitting
questions.why: Truyền thuyết nói ông nhớ vị trí ngồi của từng người.
questions.quote: he remembered where each had been sitting

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the story of Simonides?
options: It may be invented but is said to have inspired the method of loci
It has been proved by historians
It was first told by Roman orators
It describes a modern technique
questions.answer: It may be invented but is said to have inspired the method of loci
questions.why: Tác giả nói câu chuyện có thể bịa nhưng được cho là nguồn cảm hứng.
questions.quote: The story may be invented

questions.prompt: Why did Roman orators use the method of loci?
options: To win public competitions
To impress their audiences with jokes
To memorise the laws of the city
To deliver long speeches without notes
questions.answer: To deliver long speeches without notes
questions.why: Các nhà hùng biện La Mã cần diễn thuyết dài không cần ghi chú.
questions.quote: deliver long speeches without notes

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the giant loaf of bread in the example?
options: To make the route longer
To represent an item to be remembered in a striking way
To mark the end of the route
To help the speaker relax
questions.answer: To represent an item to be remembered in a striking way
questions.why: Hình ảnh nổi bật đại diện cho món cần nhớ (bánh mì trong danh sách mua sắm).
questions.quote: vivid images representing the things you want to remember

questions.prompt: Why does the method of loci work, according to the writer?
options: Brains are good at remembering places, and unusual images are easy to recall
It is practised in a quiet room
It slows down thinking
It relies on written notes
questions.answer: Brains are good at remembering places, and unusual images are easy to recall
questions.why: Hai lý do: não tiến hoá để nhớ nơi chốn và hình ảnh lạ dễ nhớ hơn từ trừu tượng.
questions.quote: Human brains evolved to remember places

questions.prompt: What did scientists find about people who compete in memory championships?
options: Their brains were larger than average
They had unusually high intelligence
Their brains were normal, but spatial-memory regions were unusually active when they memorised
They were born with perfect memories
questions.answer: Their brains were normal, but spatial-memory regions were unusually active when they memorised
questions.why: Não bình thường, IQ trung bình, nhưng vùng trí nhớ không gian hoạt động mạnh khi ghi nhớ.
questions.quote: regions linked with spatial memory became unusually active

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, 'distinguished' is closest in meaning to
options: connected
confused
protected
set apart
questions.answer: set apart
questions.why: 'What distinguished them' = điều khiến họ khác biệt.
questions.quote: What distinguished them was that

questions.prompt: What were the results of the experiment with ordinary volunteers?
options: They recalled all the words in the list
Their average recall rose from about twenty-six to about sixty-two words
Their recall fell after four months
They showed no improvement
questions.answer: Their average recall rose from about twenty-six to about sixty-two words
questions.why: Số từ nhớ trung bình tăng từ ~26 lên ~62.
questions.quote: rose from around twenty-six to around sixty-two

questions.prompt: What was notable about the improvement?
options: It disappeared quickly
It was greater for older volunteers
It was still visible four months later
It occurred only for numbers
questions.answer: It was still visible four months later
questions.why: Cải thiện vẫn còn sau bốn tháng.
questions.quote: still visible four months later

questions.prompt: What limitation of the method does the writer mention?
options: It does not help with understanding why or how things happen
It works only for numbers
It requires special equipment
It is too fast for beginners
questions.answer: It does not help with understanding why or how things happen
questions.why: Phương pháp tốt cho danh sách nhưng không giúp hiểu nguyên nhân hay cách giải.
questions.quote: it does nothing to help a student understand why a historical event happened

questions.prompt: What do some educators think about memorisation?
options: It is essential at every level
Students should be taught the method of loci
Facts should be taught only at school
It is an outdated habit
questions.answer: It is an outdated habit
questions.why: Một số nhà giáo dục gạt bỏ ghi nhớ như thói quen lỗi thời.
questions.quote: dismiss memorisation as an outdated habit

questions.prompt: How do other people reply to those educators?
options: Looking things up is faster than remembering
Facts in the mind are the raw material of creative thought
Creativity does not need knowledge
Memory is too unreliable to trust
questions.answer: Facts in the mind are the raw material of creative thought
questions.why: Phía kia cho rằng kiến thức trong đầu là nguyên liệu của tư duy sáng tạo.
questions.quote: the raw material of creative thought

questions.prompt: Why can using the same route repeatedly cause problems?
options: The route becomes shorter
The images become less vivid
Old and new images may be confused
The brain forgets the locations
questions.answer: Old and new images may be confused
questions.why: Dùng lại một tuyến dễ nhầm hình ảnh cũ và mới.
questions.quote: confusion between old and new images

questions.prompt: What did Ebbinghaus discover about forgetting?
options: It is fastest soon after learning
It is slowest soon after learning
It depends on intelligence
It is faster for nonsense syllables only
questions.answer: It is fastest soon after learning
questions.why: Ebbinghaus phát hiện quên nhanh nhất ngay sau khi học.
questions.quote: forgetting is fastest soon after learning

questions.prompt: What effect does reviewing material at increasing intervals have?
options: It makes lists longer
It flattens the forgetting curve
It removes the need for testing
It speeds up reading
questions.answer: It flattens the forgetting curve
questions.why: Ôn tập giãn cách làm đường cong quên phẳng hơn.
questions.quote: flattens this curve

questions.prompt: What did the study on retrieval practice show?
options: Students who reread remembered more
Both groups remembered equally
Students who tested themselves felt more confident
Students who tested themselves remembered more a week later
questions.answer: Students who tested themselves remembered more a week later
questions.why: Nhóm tự kiểm tra nhớ nhiều hơn dù nhóm đọc lại thấy tự tin hơn.
questions.quote: remembered more a week later than those who simply read it again

questions.prompt: In the final paragraph, 'complements' means
options: substitutes
opponents
things that work well together
earlier versions
questions.answer: things that work well together
questions.why: 'Complements rather than rivals' = bổ sung cho nhau chứ không cạnh tranh.
questions.quote: complements rather than rivals

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what does a memory palace do?
options: It gives structure to facts that must be learned in order
It improves understanding of difficult ideas
It replaces self-testing
It builds creativity directly
questions.answer: It gives structure to facts that must be learned in order
questions.why: Cung điện trí nhớ tạo cấu trúc cho dữ kiện cần học theo thứ tự.
questions.quote: gives structure to facts that must be learned in order

questions.prompt: What is the writer's final point?
options: Memory training should replace understanding
A reliably trained memory leaves more room to think about meaning
Understanding is less useful than recall
Memory apps are the best solution
questions.answer: A reliably trained memory leaves more room to think about meaning
questions.why: Câu cuối: trí nhớ được rèn giữ thông tin ổn định thì có nhiều chỗ hơn để nghĩ về ý nghĩa.
questions.quote: has more room to think about what that information means

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to memory techniques?
options: Dismissive
Uncritically enthusiastic
Neutral, giving no opinion
Positive, but realistic about their limits
questions.answer: Positive, but realistic about their limits
questions.why: Tác giả ghi nhận bằng chứng ủng hộ nhưng nhắc giới hạn và không thay thế hiểu biết.
questions.quote: None of them replaces understanding
